articles.title: Keep Claude Code, Cursor and the rest of your stack. Put Kimchi's proxy in front.
articles.excerpt: Originally published on the Kimchi blog by Gaurang Singh. Our own engineers never gave up Claude Code. What changed is the path underneath it. Their Claude Code traffic runs through Kimchi, and the Ki…
articles.body: Originally published on the Kimchi blog by Gaurang Singh. Our own engineers never gave up Claude Code. What changed is the path underneath it. Their Claude Code traffic runs through Kimchi, and the Kimchi console caps each person's Anthropic spend while open models are effectively unlimited. The cap started at $400 a month. One engineer called it "like being on a diet while having a fridge stacked with ice cream." In August we cut it to $200. Last month's usage said it would touch about one in five of us. Customers tell us the same thing from the other side. A platform lead at a 300-engineer Cursor shop put it plainly: "I don't think 300 engineers are going to put in that much effort if it's difficult." That's the point of this post.

articles.excerpt: DeepSeek Opens Its Inference Engine to the World – What the Numbers Really Mean DeepSeek just gave developers the keys to run a 67 B model on a single‑node GPU cluster. The claim sparked a flurry of h…
articles.body: DeepSeek Opens Its Inference Engine to the World – What the Numbers Really Mean The Lead DeepSeek just gave developers the keys to run a 67 B model on a single‑node GPU cluster. The claim sparked a flurry of headlines positioning the release as a direct challenge to proprietary stacks such as OpenAI’s hosted API or NVIDIA’s TensorRT‑LLM. Two weeks later the GitHub repository deepseekai/deepinfer went public, complete with an MIT‑style license, Docker images on Hugging Face, and a Python toolkit for model conversion. The community now holds the same low‑level kernels that DeepSeek uses internally, and the first benchmark data are already circulating on Reddit’s r/MachineLearning and Hacker News. But hype does not equal impact.

articles.title: We ran DeepSeek Harness against Kimchi on the same model. It lost by 22 points
articles.excerpt: Originally published on the Kimchi blog by Matas Kaminskas. DeepSeek Harness (dsh) came out on August 13, 2026. Seven weeks later it has 239,003 GitHub stars and 28.7k forks. So naturally we had to ru…
articles.body: Originally published on the Kimchi blog by Matas Kaminskas. DeepSeek Harness (dsh) came out on August 13, 2026. Seven weeks later it has 239,003 GitHub stars and 28.7k forks. So naturally we had to run it against Kimchi. What we ran dsh is DeepSeek's open-source agent runtime. The model adapter, tool registry, session log, and the agent loop itself are all plugins. It ships four presets - named compositions of tools, prompt, and persona, picked per session. We tested three: minimal (two tools and a one-sentence system prompt), standard (the full agent with all tools, planning, delegation, and web access), and creator (standard plus tools that can modify the runtime it runs on).

articles.title: Kubernetes v1.37: Memory QoS Graduates to Beta
articles.excerpt: The upgrade that changes nothing — on purpose The most important thing about Memory QoS graduating to Beta in Kubernetes v1.37 is what does not happen when you upgrade. The MemoryQoS feature gate is n…
articles.body: The upgrade that changes nothing — on purpose The most important thing about Memory QoS graduating to Beta in Kubernetes v1.37 is what does not happen when you upgrade. The MemoryQoS feature gate is now enabled by default on every v1.37 kubelet running on cgroup v2 nodes — and by default, it writes nothing. No memory.high, no memory.min, no memory.low. Your workloads run exactly as they did the day before the upgrade. That is not an accident or a half-finished feature. It is the design. And for platform operators, it is the right way to ship a mechanism that touches how the kernel treats container memory. What actually changed Memory QoS first appeared as Alpha in v1.22 and gained tiered memory reservation in v1.36.

articles.title: Database Optimization: Beyond the Basics
articles.excerpt: We've all been there: a perfectly good application, humming along, suddenly grinds to a halt. The culprit? Often, it's the database. While throwing more hardware at the problem might offer a temporary…
articles.body: We've all been there: a perfectly good application, humming along, suddenly grinds to a halt. The culprit? Often, it's the database. While throwing more hardware at the problem might offer a temporary reprieve, it's rarely a sustainable solution. True database optimization isn't about magic bullets; it's about understanding the fundamentals and applying them strategically. I've seen teams bite themselves in production by ignoring the basics, only to scramble when traffic spikes. Let's dig into some techniques that move beyond just 'adding an index' and really make a difference. The Unseen Cost of Bad Queries Before we even touch indexes, let's talk about queries. A poorly written query can negate the benefits of even the most perfectly tuned database.

articles.title: It sent gemini-2.5-pro and reported gemini-2.5-flash
articles.excerpt: A response's model field is not decoration. It is what your logs record, what your cost attribution divides by, what a router uses to pick the next call, and what a UI puts under the message. When it…
articles.body: A response's model field is not decoration. It is what your logs record, what your cost attribution divides by, what a router uses to pick the next call, and what a UI puts under the message. When it is wrong it is wrong quietly, and every downstream reader inherits it. Here is a case where two call paths of the same client disagree about that field, for the same request, on the same server reply. The measurement Two calls. Same client, same per-request model override, same reply shape — a reply that carries no model_version . One call streams, the other does not. call reported model requested model get_response(stream=True) gemini-2.5-pro gemini-2.5-pro get_response() gemini-2.5-flash gemini-2.5-pro The second row is the client's configured model, not the one this request resolved to.

articles.title: ‘It Represents an Evolution of the First-Person Shooter’ — Why Infinity Ward Is Giving Extraction Shooters Another Shot in Modern Warfare 4’s DMZ Mode
articles.excerpt: ‘It represents an evolution of the first-person shooter’ — why Infinity Ward is giving extraction shooters another shot in Modern Warfare 4’s DMZ mode.
articles.body: The last time Call of Duty attempted an extraction shooter, we were living in a world without Arc Raiders in it. The DMZ beta that came with 2022’s Modern Warfare 2 was a valiant first draft, but one that ultimately failed to hook a sizable player base with its shoot, loot, and extract loop. Now the genre’s outlook is seemingly very different, with a boom in player interest thanks to the initial success of Embark Studios’ sci-fi shooter at the back end of 2025. With its popularity not quite where it was some months ago, the jury remains out on whether extraction shooters will ever be able to topple the battle royale anytime soon, if ever. But Infinity Ward is willing to try to find that out for itself with Modern Warfare 4 and its DMZ mode — the studio’s second shot at such an idea.

articles.title: Could a $200K bond for satellites paid before launch prevent a space junk disaster in orbit? Here's why some scientists think so
articles.excerpt: The space around Earth is turning into a junkyard. Researchers think a refundable deposit scheme could force satellite operators to clean up their act before a tipping point is reached.
articles.body: The space around Earth is turning into a junkyard. Researchers think a refundable deposit scheme could force satellite operators to clean up their act before a tipping point is reached. For years, space sustainability experts have warned that the growing number of satellites in orbit and the quantity of dead metal left behind threatens to trigger a dangerous cascade of collisions known as the Kessler Syndrome . Predicted in the 1970s by NASA physicist Donald Kessler, this chain of orbital smashups could make the space around Earth unusable and unsafe. The dangerous tipping might be nearer than some think.
articles.author: Tereza Pultarova

articles.title: AI adoption by industry shows what other sectors can learn
articles.excerpt: The current narrative around artificial intelligence in the workplace is largely driven by Silicon Valley. But treating the tech sector as an island misses the actual trends in technology adoption–tec…
articles.body: The current narrative around artificial intelligence in the workplace is largely driven by Silicon Valley. But treating the tech sector as an island misses the actual trends in technology adoption–tech is just the first industry in line. As generative AI and automation tools mature, the shifts currently reshaping software engineering and product management will inevitably filter into healthcare, education, retail, and manufacturing. The variation in adoption rates today isn’t a sign that non-tech industries are falling behind, but rather a reflection of the different speeds at which industries absorb new workflows. For leaders and their teams outside of tech, this differential pace provides a practical blueprint for how AI adoption unfolds, and where the opportunities lie.
articles.author: TripleTen

articles.title: SpaceX launches its 'Starfall' return capsule for 2nd time ever (video)
articles.excerpt: SpaceX launched its Starfall return capsule for the second time ever this morning (Oct. 20), sending it up on the Bandwagon-5 rideshare mission.
articles.body: SpaceX just launched its mysterious "Starfall" return capsule for the second time ever. Starfall was one of 32 payloads on the company's Bandwagon-5 rideshare mission, which launched atop a Falcon 9 rocket at 7:04 a.m. EDT (1104 GMT) today (Oct. 20) from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. SpaceX has been relatively quiet about Starfall, which debuted this past June on a Falcon 9 launch from the Cape. The payloads of SpaceX's Bandwagon-5 rideshare mission, seen in a prelaunch photo. The company's Starfall capsule sits at the very top of the stack. (Image credit: SpaceX) That June 23 flight was a dedicated demonstration mission for Starfall, designed to show that the capsule can fly in a controlled fashion and survive the harrowing downward trip through Earth's atmosphere .
articles.author: Mike Wall

articles.title: NASA closes the book on epic OSIRIS-REx asteroid-sampling mission: 'I am immensely proud of what we did'
articles.excerpt: NASA's OSIRIS-REx asteroid-sampling mission formally ended on Sept. 30, 2026, though scientists will continue to study the pieces of space rock it returned for decades.
articles.body: On Sept. 30, NASA formally concluded OSIRIS-REx, the historic first U.S. mission to pluck a pristine piece of an asteroid and deliver it safely back to Earth. The van-sized OSIRIS-REx spacecraft — whose name is short for Origins, Spectral Interpretation, Resource Identification, Security-Regolith Explorer — visited and sampled Bennu , an ancient space rock holding pristine remnants from the dawn of our solar system more than 4.5 billion years ago. Among those cosmic relics are raw organic building blocks , the kind that may have seeded life on Earth. "I have known this day was coming for a long time, but it is still difficult to see it arrive," OSIRIS-REx Principal Investigator Dante Lauretta, who's based at the University of Arizona, said in a post on LinkedIn .

articles.title: A visit to Samsung’s massive new semiconductor hub
articles.excerpt: Generative AI models run on powerful chips known as GPUs, which depend on stacks of specialized memory chips packaged with the processor. To meet growing demand for memory, Samsung is building a massi…
articles.body: _____________ THE PLACE Pyeongtaek, South Korea Generative AI models run on powerful chips known as GPUs, which depend on stacks of specialized memory chips packaged with the processor. To meet growing demand for memory, Samsung is building a massive new semiconductor manufacturing complex in Pyeongtaek, South Korea. Three fabs already operate around the clock, and a fourth is coming online. Construction of a fifth was halted during a drop in demand for memory chips in 2024 but restarted when the AI boom sent demand soaring. It’s just before noon on a Monday, and construction workers are pouring out of Samsung’s fabs in Pyeongtaek, a farming city south of Seoul where rice paddies abut a sprawling chipmaking complex.
